title: Children's services budget increase and Doon reopening
subtitle: Also: SHIP supportive housing, youth survey, community paramedicine funding, rabies program update and Mooregate tenant engagement.
overview: The committee recommended that Council increase the 2026 Children's Services operating budget by $7,879,158 to reflect changes in Ministry of Education funding. The change has no net tax levy impact, so it does not add to property taxes. It was part of the consent agenda, which the committee approved {{vote:m1}}.

The committee also heard several reports and received them for information. Staff said Doon Heritage Village will reopen on July 1, 2026, after closing in 2023 for infrastructure and accessibility upgrades. Staff will bring back information to Council on free admission for Canada Day. The committee also heard that the Community Paramedicine Program, which is fully provincially funded, has grown to nine full-time paramedics. It heard about the fourth Youth Impact Survey, open to youth aged 9 to 18 through May, and a presentation from SHIP on its housing programs.

Under other business, a commissioner said staff have sent follow-up communication about the postponed Mooregate project and are willing to hold more engagement sessions with relocated tenants and neighbours, working with the ward councillor. The next meeting is June 2, 2026.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council raise the 2026 Children's Services operating budget by $7,879,158, with $0 net tax levy impact, to reflect changed Ministry of Education funding for child care.

The committee approved the consent agenda {{vote:m1}}, which included receiving the 2025 rabies prevention and control program update for information and the child care funding report behind the budget recommendation.

debate: On Doon Heritage Village, one councillor asked why the report did not show the village's annual budget, saying the public should see the cost. Staff said it is not budgeted as a separate unit, and the Chief Financial Officer put its net operating cost at roughly $700,000 a year.
The same councillor suggested making Canada Day admission free instead of the planned $2 fee, citing affordability pressures. Staff agreed to take the idea away and report back to Council.

On community paramedicine, councillors were concerned that provincial funding is held steady for 2026-27 just as the program plans to expand. One suggested taking advocacy to the AMO conference. Staff said they would explore options, and councillors noted that frontline referrals reduce emergency department visits.

SHIP delegates said reliable funding is the main challenge and that they expect to return at budget time. Councillors asked how Council can best help, how the programs are funded and how long clients can stay.

On the Youth Impact Survey, one councillor asked whether young people could use it to voice concerns about provincial policy such as tuition. Staff said the questions are general, but an open-ended question at the end allows specific comments.
